claims.text: Periodic potential pulses induce reversible surface segregation in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalysts during ethanol oxidation.
Pulse-induced surface segregation enhances ethanol-oxidation activity.
Pulse-induced surface segregation improves ethanol-oxidation selectivity.
The segregation enriches active metal sites such as Pt at the catalyst surface.
The initial PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst has a random atomic distribution across its surface.
Potential pulses trigger transient atomic rearrangements in the catalyst.
Metals having favorable oxidation or binding energies selectively migrate to the surface during pulsing.
Changes in surface composition adjust the adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Changing intermediate adsorption through surface-composition changes boosts catalytic performance.
Pulsed operation will increase ethanol-oxidation current density relative to constant-potential operation.
Pulsed operation will alter the product distribution and improve selectivity relative to constant-potential operation.
The performance changes will occur concomitantly with transient surface enrichment of an active element.
The hypothesis is intended to apply in 0.1 M HClO4 containing 0.5 M ethanol at 25–80 °C.
The hypothesis applies only within a potential window that allows reversible restructuring without irreversible oxidation or dissolution.
Operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy can be used to detect reaction-induced element-specific structural or compositional changes.
In situ infrared spectroscopy can monitor adsorbed intermediates during the proposed ethanol-oxidation experiment.
